texts.07f3ea45e5bc: A randomised controlled trial of extended warfarin treatment versus routine warfarin treatment for the prevention of recurrent VTE and post thrombotic syndrome in patients being treated for a first episode of unprovoked VTE. This study aims to:  i) Identify patients at highest risk of having a second clot from D-dimer tests and other factors;  ii) See if extended treatment can prevent recurrent clots;  iii) Identify patients at highest risk of developing post thrombotic syndrome;  iv) Identify the most cost-effective means of both preventing and treating clots;  v) Determine patient preferences and utilities with regard to extended warfarin Background Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is the umbrella term given to blood clots in the lungs and legs. It is a common condition associated with high morbidity and mortality. After having a clot, a few people are at very high risk of having another one, and there is a slight risk of a clot in the lungs leading to serious lung damage, or even death. In the longer term, patients may also develop problems with circulation in their legs, known as post thrombotic syndrome. At present, treatment with warfarin, a blood thinning drug, is generally stopped after 3 to 6 months, because many patients will not develop another clot and warfarin can cause problems, especially with bleeding. However, recurrence after first unprovoked DVT can be up to 10% per annum following treatment cessation irrespective of the duration of anticoagulation therapy. Clearly some patients need long-term anticoagulation, but we are currently unable to identify this population. How you will use the data we supply. Patients who are receiving warfarin for a first unprovoked blood clot will be identified by the anticoagulation specialist nurses in 7 secondary care sites. Eligible patients will be given an information sheet and a prepaid consent post card indicating their initial interest in taking part. The GPs of patients who send back positive replies will be contacted and asked to give their consent to the GP practice being involved in the study. The GP will also be asked to indicate if there are any reasons why the interested patient cannot take part. Patients will be sent a reminder letter one month before their due date for discontinuing warfarin and an invitation letter to attend their GP surgery for an appointment with a research nurse 2 weeks prior to their warfarin discontinuing. For those patients who want to take part, but their GP practice does not give consent, alternative arrangements will be made for the patient to participate at the anticoagulation clinic where they were initially informed about the study. At the first appointment with the researcher, patients will be given further information about the study and asked to give their written consent. Patients will then be interviewed about their medical history and their medical notes will be reviewed and they will be clinically examined for signs of post thrombotic syndrome. A venous blood sample will be taken, Patients will be asked to complete two Quality of Life questionnaires. The research nurse will then enter the patient details into a computer system, which will randomise patients to either continue warfarin for a further 2 years or to discontinue treatment. All patients will be in the study for 2 years after they are randomised to a group, with review appointments every 6 months. At the 6 monthly reviews patients randomised to both groups will be assessed for evidence of recurrence of DVT and post thrombotic syndrome. All patients will also be asked to complete two Quality of Life measures at each of the 6 monthly reviews. Patients randomly allocated to continue warfarin will be followed up through their usual oral anticoagulation service provided in terms of warfarin management, and will therefore have regular INR checks. An intention to treat analysis will be used and analysis will be carried out at the end of the study, as there is likely to be insufficient power for interim analyses. Any patients lost to follow up will be traced through MRIS. Prior to each six monthly visit the current health status of patients will also be obtained from MRIS information.
